food.text: Surströmming, a lightly salted, fermented Baltic Sea herring, has been part of Swedish cuisine since at least the 16th century. Just enough salt is used to keep the raw herring from rotting while it ferments. A fermentation of at least six months gives the fish a somewhat acidic taste and one of the most putrid food smells in the world, stronger than that of the Korean hongeo-hoe, the Japanese kusaya or the Icelandic hákarl.

Cattle rearing was widespread in Scandinavia, especially Denmark, where the Black Death had left huge field areas untended and well suited for grazing. An export market for high-grade beef slowly built up after the 1360s, and by the 17th century it had reached well over 100,000 animals per year. Butter was also a major export product.
The devastating Great Famine of 1695 to 1697 struck Finland, then part of Sweden, and one-third of the Finnish population died. Famine also hit Sweden itself, killing roughly 10% of its population.
Brännvin, the Nordic distilled liquor, has been produced in Sweden since the late 15th century. Total production was still small in the 17th century, but from the early 18th century it expanded.

In the 16th century, Swedish and Finnish merchants and upper-class households served a small buffet on a snaps table, called a brännvinsbord. The simplest version offered bread, butter, cheese, herring and several liqueurs. It was eaten standing, often two to five hours before dinner.

In the 16th century, Russian and Swedish stockfish were sold to many European countries. Stockfish is unsalted fish, especially cod, dried by cold air and wind on wooden racks. Dried fish has a storage life of several years.
The Danish and Swedish East India Companies imported more tea than the British East India Company during their heyday. They smuggled 90% of it into Britain, where it could be sold at a huge profit.

The Swedish phrase att bre(da) smörgåsar, meaning to spread butter on open-faced sandwiches, has been used since at least the 16th century. The smörgås of smörgåsbord gets its name from gås, which literally meant goose but later came to refer to the small pieces of butter that floated to the surface of cream as it was churned.

Potatoes started to be used to make Swedish brännvin in the late 18th century. They became the dominant ingredient from the early 19th century, replacing the grain that the spirit had first been made from.

art.text: The Reformation greatly disrupted Danish artistic traditions. It left the existing body of painters and sculptors without large markets for their work.

In Denmark, the court and aristocracy mainly wanted portraits, and these were usually made by imported artists. It was not until the 18th century that large numbers of Danes were trained in contemporary styles.

The Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts was established in 1754, following the general European pattern. It was intended to develop a national school and reduce the need to import artists from other countries.
tags: Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts

art.text: From the late 18th century, the situation for Danish art changed radically. Beginning with the Danish Golden Age, a distinct tradition of Danish art began and has continued to flourish until today.

Johannes Wiedewelt was a Neoclassical sculptor trained in Italy and France, who followed his father as court sculptor. He directed the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts from 1772 to 1777 and from 1780 to 1789. He is remembered for the monument of King Frederick V in Roskilde Cathedral and the Naval Monument in Holmens Cemetery.
tags: Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts

art.text: The first painter to lead the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts was the Swedish-born Carl Gustaf Pilo (c. 1711 to 1793). He was a portraitist and history painter in the grand style.
tags: Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts

art.text: The Royal Copenhagen Porcelain Factory was established in 1775 as a royal initiative, typical of monarchies in the period. The business has outlasted the great majority of such factories and survives today as part of a larger group.

The rise of the Swedish Empire in the seventeenth century began a flourishing of Swedish art. It also brought the founding of the notable Swedish royal art collection, and painters established themselves internationally with portraits for the wealthy nobility and monarchy.
Nikolaj Abraham Abildgaard (1743 to 1809) led the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts after Carl Gustaf Pilo. He was himself an ex-student of the Academy, and he developed a Neo-Classical style.
tags: Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts

art.text: Most leading Danish artists for at least a century after the Academy's founding trained there and often returned to teach. Christian August Lorentzen and Jens Juel were among those who taught there, and Juel later became Director too. The tension between academic art and other styles was much less a feature of Danish art history than of France or England.
tags: Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts

art.text: The Kosta Glasbruk glass company was founded in 1742 by two army officers. It later became part of the same group as the Royal Copenhagen Porcelain Factory, and it is known internationally.
In the eighteenth century, the painter Alexander Roslin had a strong role within European art. He was one of the leading painters as the classical tradition expanded further in Sweden.

Two extensively decorated horns of sheet gold, the Golden Horns of Gallehus, were discovered in Southern Jutland in 1639 and 1734. The larger horn shows two animal-headed men facing each other, armed with what appears to be a sickle and a wood-splitting axe. They are dated to the early 5th century and could represent something related to berserkers.

war.text: The Northern Seven Years' War was fought from 1563 to 1570 between Sweden and a coalition of Denmark–Norway, Lübeck and Poland–Lithuania. Fighting continued until both armies had been exhausted, and many men died. The Treaty of Stettin ended it as a stalemate, with neither side gaining any new territory.

The Great Northern War pitted a coalition of Russia, Denmark–Norway and Saxony-Poland against Sweden from 1700 to 1721. It ended with the Treaty of Nystad and the Stockholm treaties. As a result, Russia replaced Sweden as the dominant power on the Baltic Sea and became a major player in European politics.

In 1625 Christian IV of Denmark–Norway, a Lutheran, led an army against the Holy Roman Empire to help German Protestants. He invaded at the head of a mercenary army of 20,000 men, but the Danish forces were severely beaten. He had to sign an ignominious defeat, the first in a series of military setbacks that weakened his kingdom.

In 1520 Christian II of Denmark reconquered Sweden and took a bloody revenge on the anti-Union faction at the Stockholm Bloodbath. More than 80 noble men and ladies, including leading citizens of Stockholm, were executed. The violence severely backfired on him, provoking strong reactions in Sweden for years to come.

The Northern Seven Years' War was motivated by the dissatisfaction of King Frederick II of Denmark with the dissolution of the Kalmar Union. King Eric XIV of Sweden, for his part, wanted to break Denmark's dominating position.

At sea the Swedes fared better in the Northern Seven Years' War. Their admiral Horn pursued a Danish–Lübeck fleet onto the German coast, where most of it was destroyed. He then steered for Öresund and levied a toll on passing ships.

The Kalmar Union was broken by the successful Swedish War of Liberation, fought from 1521 to 1523. Christian II was condemned by the Pope and abdicated in 1523. The Danish kings who followed, Frederick I and Christian III, focused mainly on the Reformation and the Count's Feud civil war, so relations with Sweden were generally peaceful.

On 7 July 1565 the Swedish navy under Horn defeated a Danish–Lübeck navy under Otto Rud near Bornholm. Sweden captured the Danish flagship, the Jegermesther. This ensured Swedish command of the eastern Baltic that year.

On land, Nils Boije took Varberg on 28 August 1564 after King Eric turned over command of the Swedish army to him. The Danish army under Daniel Rantzau then beat the Swedes at the Battle of Axtorna on 20 October 1565.

Christian IV had profited from his policies in northern Germany, and his kingdom enjoyed stability and wealth paid for by the Øresund toll and war reparations from Sweden. It also helped that the French regent Cardinal Richelieu was willing to pay for a Danish incursion into Germany.

At the Battle at Buchow on 4 June 1565, on the Mecklenburg coast, the Danish–Lübeck commander Herluf Trolle was mortally wounded. It was one of several clashes that made 1565 a hard year at sea for the Danish–Lübeck side.

In January 1566 Sweden unsuccessfully besieged Bohus Fortress in Bohuslän, then a Norwegian province. On 28 July a storm at sea destroyed half of the Danish–Lübeck navy. Horn, called to command troops on land, died on 9 September.

literature.text: A full Swedish translation of the Bible appeared in 1541, made possible by the printing press. It is possibly the most significant Swedish book of all time. It introduced the common man to a language beyond the everyday, and churches used it for around 400 years.

Sixteenth-century Swedish writing gave rise to Gothicism. This movement held that the Goths, a renowned East Germanic tribe, originated from Scandinavia, and Sweden in particular. Its influence showed up in several works during the 17th century.

The Lutheran Reformation reached Denmark in the 16th century and opened a new period in its literature. The humanist Christiern Pedersen translated the New Testament into Danish, while Poul Helgesen vigorously opposed the Reformation.

In 1665–1668, the first novel in Swedish was published. The 17th century also saw the first Swedish poetry books, and Georg Stiernhielm's poetry collection was one of the first of major importance in Swedish.

The deposed Swedish archbishop Johannes Magnus lived in exile in Rome from 1530 to 1544 with his brother Olaus Magnus. In Historia de omnibus gothorum suenumque regibus (1554), he traced the Swedish line of kings back to the Old Testament. The brothers' works gained attention throughout Europe and were translated into several languages.
tags: Historia de omnibus gothorum suenumque regibus

literature.text: The first official Swedish hymn book was published in 1695 and is attributed to bishop Jesper Svedberg, assisted by Haqvin Spegel. Its plain language gave commoners greater access to a standardized language. It stayed beloved in sermons all over Sweden for a full century, until a new hymn book in 1819.

Leonora Christina of the Blue Tower chronicles Denmark's struggles with Sweden and the noble rivalries that led to absolute monarchy in 1660. It does so from the redemptive perspective of a royal prisoner, in heartfelt prose.

In the late 17th century, Swedish scholars began first publications of legendary sagas, with Latin and Swedish translations, to support Sweden's "noble past" and "Age of Greatness". Olaus Verelius published Hervarar saga in 1672, and Johan Peringskiöld published the Heimskringla in 1697.
Olof Rudbeck was the main representative of non-fiction in the 17th century. He popularized Swedish Gothicism with his work Atlantica.
Religious dogmatism was on the rise in 17th-century Denmark. Even so, the passionate hymns of Thomas Kingo transcended the genre with personal expression.

In 1737, Eric Julius Björner published the collection Nordiska kämpadater, which included the Völsunga saga, Hrólfs saga kraka and Ragnars saga loðbrókar. Johan Göransson then published the Prose Edda in Latin in 1746.
Johan Peringskiöld's son, Johan Fredrik Peringskiöld, kept up the work of publishing old sagas. He brought out Sögubrot af nokkrum fornkonungum in 1719 and Ásmundar saga kappabana in 1722.

science.text: Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg between about 1576 and 1580 on Ven, an island in the Öresund that was part of Denmark at the time. It was the first custom-built observatory in modern Europe, and the last to be built without a telescope as its primary instrument.

In 1736, Anders Celsius joined a French Academy of Sciences expedition to Lapland, led by Pierre Louis Maupertuis, to measure a degree of latitude near the pole. The result was compared with a similar expedition to Peru near the equator. The expeditions confirmed Isaac Newton's belief that the Earth is an ellipsoid flattened at the poles.

In 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer first demonstrated that light travels at a finite speed. Studying Jupiter's moon Io, he estimated that light takes about 11 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth. That works out to roughly 220,000 kilometers per second, compared with today's accepted value of 299,792.

Carl Linnaeus, a Swedish biologist and physician, formalised binomial nomenclature, the modern system of naming organisms. He lived abroad between 1735 and 1738 and published the first edition of his Systema Naturae in the Netherlands. He later became professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala.

Anders Celsius proposed his temperature scale in 1742 in a paper to the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala. His thermometer was calibrated with 0 for the boiling point of water and 100 for the freezing point. In 1745, a year after his death, Carl Linnaeus reversed the scale to make measurement more practical.
tags: Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala

science.text: By 1659, the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno seriously questioned accepted knowledge of the natural world. He doubted explanations for tear production, the idea that fossils grew in the ground, and explanations of rock formation. Scholars now consider him one of the founders of modern stratigraphy and modern geology.

While tracking the comet of 1577, Tycho Brahe saw inaccuracies in the star positions of both Ptolemy's and Copernicus's systems. In 1588 he released the Tychonic system, with Earth stationary at the center, the Moon and Sun revolving around it, and the five planets revolving around the Sun. Paul Wittich helped him after visiting Uraniborg in 1580.
In 1700, Ole Rømer persuaded the king to introduce the Gregorian calendar in Denmark and Norway. Tycho Brahe had argued for the same change in vain a hundred years earlier.

In 1585, Tycho Brahe created a larger instrument called the Great Equatorial Armillary to gauge planetary and stellar positions. He used it extensively in 1587 to work on the parallax of Mars, which he had tried and failed to calculate in 1582, 1583, and 1585. Its measurements still led to unprecedented accuracy.

Anders Celsius studied auroras with his assistant Olof Hiorter. He observed a compass needle and found that larger deflections went with stronger auroral activity, making him the first to suggest a link between the aurora borealis and changes in the Earth's magnetic field. At Nuremberg in 1733, he published 316 aurora observations.

In 1716, Emanuel Swedenborg met King Charles XII in Lund, hoping to persuade him to fund an observatory in northern Sweden. The Swedish inventor Christopher Polhem, a close friend, was also present. The warlike king did not think the project important enough, but appointed Swedenborg assessor-extraordinary on the Swedish Board of Mines.

For his Uppsala observatory, Anders Celsius had the university consistory buy a large stone house of medieval origin in central Uppsala. He had the observatory built on its rooftop and also lived in the house. The rooftop observatory was demolished in 1857, though the Celsius house still stands.

politics.text: The Great Northern War pitted Sweden against a coalition of Russia, Denmark–Norway and Saxony-Poland, with Prussia and Hanover joining from 1715. It began with a coordinated attack on Sweden in 1700 and ended in 1721 with the Treaty of Nystad and the Stockholm treaties. Russia supplanted Sweden as the dominant Baltic power.

The three Scandinavian kingdoms had joined in 1397 in the Kalmar Union. Sweden left it in 1523 under King Gustav I of Sweden. Civil war then broke out in Denmark and Norway, and the Protestant Reformation followed.

The borders between Denmark, Norway and Sweden took their present shape in the mid-17th century. In the 1645 Treaty of Brömsebro, Denmark–Norway ceded Jämtland, Härjedalen, Idre and Särna, plus the Baltic islands of Gotland and Ösel, to Sweden.
Denmark and Norway entered a personal union in 1536 that lasted until 1814. The Norwegian privy council had assembled for the last time in 1537, after which it was abolished.

The 1658 Treaty of Roskilde forced Denmark–Norway to cede Scania, Blekinge, Halland, Bornholm, Båhuslen and Trøndelag to Sweden. The 1660 Treaty of Copenhagen forced Sweden to return Bornholm and Trøndelag to Denmark–Norway, and to give up its recent claims to the island Funen.

Christian IV of Denmark–Norway, himself a Lutheran, led an army against the Holy Roman Empire from 1625 to 1629 to help German Protestants. He feared Denmark's sovereignty as a Protestant nation was threatened. His mercenary army of 20,000 men was severely beaten, and he had to sign an ignominious defeat.

Denmark started a Caribbean colony on St Thomas in 1671 and on St John in 1718. It purchased Saint Croix from France in 1733. Sweden had briefly held New Sweden in Delaware in the 1630s and later acquired Saint-Barthélemy in 1785.
Sweden became the first country with a law explicitly protecting freedom of the press. This came during the eighteenth century, an age when Swedish culture flourished.

Christian IV had gained a level of stability and wealth for his kingdom that was virtually unmatched elsewhere in Europe. It was paid for by the Øresund toll and extensive war reparations from Sweden. The French regent Cardinal Richelieu was even willing to pay for a Danish incursion into Germany.

Denmark–Norway apparently believed the Norse settlements in Greenland still survived, so it kept claiming sovereignty over the island. In 1721 it sent a missionary expedition to restore Christianity among the settlers' descendants. No Norse were found, and the missionaries baptized the Inuit instead.

From 1605 to 1607, King Christian IV of Denmark financed three expeditions to learn the fate of the Greenland colonists. They did not find the settlements again. Captain Gerd Mestemaker had reached the west coast in 1541 but found no one alive there.

The Swedish and Norwegian boundaries were agreed and marked out in 1751. It was not until the middle of the 17th century that Sweden had a secure outlet on the Kattegat and control of the south Baltic coast.

philosophy.text: Philosophy was the first academic subject in Finland, and in the world as well. When the Royal Academy of Turku was founded in 1640, professors of law, medicine and theology were appointed alongside those of philosophical sciences.

Witch trials faded across much of Europe by the mid-17th century but continued on its fringes. In the Nordic countries, the late 17th century saw the peak of the trials in a number of areas, including Swedish Finland.
philosophy.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

philosophy.text: Norse mythology has been the subject of scholarly discourse since the 17th century, when key texts attracted the attention of the intellectual circles of Europe. Later scholars used comparative mythology and historical linguistics to trace elements of Germanic mythology back to Proto-Indo-European mythology.
At the start, the Royal Academy of Turku's Faculty of Philosophical Sciences had four professorships. They covered ethics, political doctrine and history; logic and poetry; mathematics; and rhetoric.
After the Reformation, Finns who wanted training went mainly to Germany. There the University of Wittenberg had become the centre of Protestant theology.

In the Torsåker witch trials of Sweden in 1674, 71 people were executed for witchcraft in a single day. The event stands as one of the peaks of Nordic witch hunting in the late 17th century, alongside the peak of witch hunting in Swedish Finland.
philosophy.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

philosophy.text: The first two professorships at Turku, ethics with political doctrine and history, and logic with poetry, included the study and teaching of philosophy. They can be considered to correspond to today's fields of practical and theoretical philosophy.

The 17th century Icelandic Galdrabók grimoire contains spells that sometimes make references to Norse mythology. So does a medieval charm recorded as used by the Norwegian woman Ragnhild Tregagås, who was convicted of witchcraft in Norway in the 14th century. Both are later sources reaching into the modern period that still refer to Norse mythology.

culture.text: In the 16th century, Sweden left the Catholic community and assumed the Lutheran faith. King Gustav I had wrested the throne from Christian II of Denmark and promoted a national church headed by himself.

In the 18th century, Swedish culture flourished. Carl Linnaeus had a vast impact on biology and promoted widespread interest in the topic, while Carl Michael Bellman produced many significant songs and poems.
Under Gustav I, the whole Bible was translated into Swedish for the first time. That translation came to serve as a norm for the Swedish language.

Queen Louisa Ulrika and her son King Gustav III were important patrons of the arts, both founding academies that are still active. Gustav III also established the Swedish Academy and founded the Nationalmuseum in the eighteenth century.

The 17th century saw a rise in interest in the history of Sweden, with the establishment of the Swedish National Heritage Board as one example. Sweden also appeared as a champion of the Protestant cause, while plundering foreign cultural riches during the Thirty Years War.
